--- title: "Hands-on Exercise 5a" subtitle: "Visual Correlation Analysis" author: "Jedidiah Asaf T" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true --- ## Overview This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 6 of *R for Visual Analytics*. The focus is on building **correlation matrices and corrgrams** to reveal the pairwise relationships among the physicochemical properties of wine, using `corrplot` and `ggstatsplot`. ## Setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman") pacman::p_load( corrplot, ggstatsplot, tidyverse ) wine <- read_csv("data/wine_quality.csv") ``` ::: ## Data Preview ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DT::datatable( head(wine, 50), class = "compact", options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # 1. Building a Correlation Matrix with `pairs()` ## 1.1 Basic Scatterplot Matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine[, 1:11]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 1.2 Lower-corner Only Showing only the lower half removes the redundant mirror image. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 1.3 Showing the Correlation Coefficient A custom `panel.cor()` function prints the absolute correlation in the upper panel, sized by strength. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) { usr <- par("usr") on.exit(par(usr)) par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1)) r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")) txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1] txt <- paste0(prefix, txt) if (missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt) text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2) } pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = panel.cor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` parameter ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # 2. Corrgram with ggstatsplot ## 2.1 `ggcorrmat()` `ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat()` draws the correlation coefficients and marks the statistically non-significant pairs with a cross. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine, cor.vars = 1:11 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## 2.2 Grouped Corrgram by Wine Type ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grouped_ggcorrmat( data = wine, cor.vars = 1:11, grouping.var = type, plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: # 3. Corrgram with corrplot ## 3.1 Computing and Plotting the Correlation Matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11]) corrplot(wine.cor) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 3.2 Changing the Visual Element Using ellipses and showing only the lower half. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot( wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 3.3 Mixed Layout Ellipses in the lower half, coefficients in the upper half. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot.mixed( wine.cor, lower = "ellipse", upper = "number", tl.pos = "lt", diag = "l", tl.col = "black" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 3.4 Combining with a Significance Test Pairs whose correlation is not significant at the 0.05 level are left blank. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine.sig <- cor.mtest(wine[, 1:11], conf.level = 0.95) corrplot( wine.cor, method = "number", type = "lower", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, p.mat = wine.sig$p, sig.level = 0.05 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 3.5 Reordering with Hierarchical Clustering `corrplot` can reorder the variables so that strongly correlated groups sit together, with cluster rectangles drawn on top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot( wine.cor, method = "ellipse", tl.pos = "lt", tl.col = "black", order = "hclust", hclust.method = "ward.D", addrect = 3 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hands_on_exercise_5a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # Learning Reflection In this exercise, I learned that a correlation matrix is far easier to read as a **corrgram** than as a table of numbers. `pairs()` gives a quick raw look, but `ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat()` adds real value by flagging non-significant relationships, and `grouped_ggcorrmat()` lets me compare red and white wine side by side. `corrplot` is the most flexible: reordering by hierarchical clustering and drawing cluster rectangles turned a noisy 11×11 matrix into clear blocks of related chemical properties.
